n: Josiah became king at eight and reigned thirty-one years (about 640–609 BC). His reign was the last great revival before Judah’s fall.

f.g: His birth and reforms were prophesied about 300 years earlier.

n: He did right and followed David’s ways, turning neither right nor left — steady, unwavering obedience.

f.w: declined neither to the right hand, nor to the left

n: At sixteen (his eighth year), while still young, he began to seek David’s God. At twenty he began purging Judah and Jerusalem of high places, Asherah poles, and idols. Personal conversion came first, then public reform.
In his presence they tore down Baal altars and incense altars, crushed the idols to dust, and scattered the dust on the graves of those who had worshipped them.
He burned the bones of pagan priests on their own altars, defiling those altars forever — exactly as a prophet had foretold three centuries earlier. Thus he cleansed Judah and Jerusalem.

f.w: he burnt the bones of the priests upon their altars

n: He extended his reform north into the old territories of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and Naphtali — lands of the former northern kingdom, now weakened Assyrian provinces.

f.g: The Hebrew is uncertain; often read ‘in their ruins round about.’

n: After destroying altars, poles, and idols throughout the land of Israel, he returned to Jerusalem.

f.w: beaten the graven images into powder

n: In his eighteenth year (about 622 BC), having cleansed land and temple, he sent officials to repair the Lord’s house.

f.g: A royal secretary whose family later protected the prophet Jeremiah.

n: They delivered to Hilkiah the high priest the money collected by Levite doorkeepers from Manasseh, Ephraim, the rest of Israel, Judah, and Benjamin — a nationwide offering.
The money was given to supervisors who paid the workers repairing the temple.
Carpenters and builders used it to buy cut stone and timber for beams and to rebuild what earlier kings had let decay.
The workers labored faithfully under Levite overseers from Merari and Kohath, including skilled musicians.

f.g: Honestly — no accounting was required of them.

n: Levites also supervised the laborers and served as scribes, officials, and gatekeepers.
While taking out the money, Hilkiah found the book of the Lord’s law given through Moses — likely a scroll of Deuteronomy, lost or hidden during Manasseh’s long apostasy.

f.w: a book of the law of the LORD given by Moses
f.g: Many scholars identify it with Deuteronomy or a core of it, based on Josiah’s reforms.

n: Hilkiah told Shaphan, “I found the book of the law in the temple,” and gave it to him. Lost scripture recovered is a theme Latter-day Saints know well.

f.w: I have found the book of the law

n: Shaphan brought the book to the king and first reported that the work was going as ordered.
He reported that the money had been given to the overseers and workers.
Then, almost as an afterthought, Shaphan mentioned the book and read it aloud to the king.
Hearing God’s law, Josiah tore his clothes in grief — realizing how far Judah had strayed. Scripture pricked his heart.

f.g: Tearing garments was a sign of grief and repentance.

n: Josiah sent five trusted officials, including Hilkiah and Shaphan’s son Ahikam, on an urgent mission.
He told them: inquire of the Lord for me and for those left in Israel and Judah about this book, for His great anger is upon us because our fathers didn’t obey it.

f.w: them that are left in Israel
f.g: The remnant of the northern tribes after the Assyrian exile.

n: They went to the prophetess Huldah, who lived in Jerusalem’s newer quarter. Her husband was keeper of the royal or priestly wardrobe. God spoke through a faithful woman prophet.

f.g: Hebrew mishneh — the ‘second quarter,’ a newer district of Jerusalem.

n: Huldah answered with authority: “Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, tell the man who sent you…”
God will bring disaster on Jerusalem and its people — all the curses written in the book read to the king.

f.w: all the curses that are written in the book

n: Because they abandoned Him and worshipped other gods, His wrath would pour out and not be quenched. The judgment was now certain.
But to the king who sent you to ask the Lord, say this concerning the words he has heard:
Because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself, tore your clothes, and wept before Me when you heard My words, I have heard you. A tender heart moves God.
You will die in peace and not see the disaster. The messengers reported back to the king. (Josiah died in battle, but before Jerusalem’s destruction.)

f.w: gathered to thy grave in peace
f.g: Josiah would not live to see Jerusalem’s fall, though he died in battle.

n: Rather than giving up, the king called together all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem. Even knowing judgment was coming, he chose to lead his people to God.
Josiah went to the temple with everyone — priests, Levites, and people great and small — and read aloud the whole book of the covenant. The king himself became a teacher of scripture.
Standing in the king’s place, he made a covenant before the Lord to follow Him and keep His commandments with all his heart and soul.
He had everyone in Jerusalem and Benjamin commit to it, and they lived by God’s covenant.
Josiah removed every abomination from Israel’s lands and led everyone to serve the Lord. As long as he lived, they did not turn away. But the reform seems to have depended heavily on him.
